oil.summary: Crude surged more than 7% today — WTI settling near $85.16 and Brent at $90.53 — driven by a sharp escalation in Middle East hostilities. Trump threatened Iran directly, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia struck Iran-backed militias in Iraq, and Houthis claimed an attack on a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea, compounding existing Hormuz disruption. Iran maintained its oil blockade stance, rejecting a diplomatic off-ramp. A bullish EIA print — U.S. crude inventories down 7.2 million barrels for the week ending July 24 — added fundamental support. RBOB gasoline was a notable outlier, falling 3.7% on the day, suggesting demand-side softness even as distillates held firm (Heating Oil +1.4%). Senate progress on a Russia-Iran sanctions bill introduced further tail-risk premium. The one-month gain now stands at over 20% for WTI.
drivers: Geopolitical shock: U.S.-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed Iraqi militias and Houthi attack on Saudi tanker dramatically widened the conflict perimeter
EIA inventory draw of 7.2 million barrels tightened the fundamental backdrop amid ongoing Hormuz disruption
Senate agreement on sweeping Russia-Iran sanctions bill, including proposed 500% tariffs, added structural supply-risk premium

gas.summary: Natural gas markets delivered a split session. TTF rose 4.79% to €60.5/MWh — up 42% on the month — as Hormuz tensions kept European buyers on edge over potential LNG supply disruptions. ADNOC confirmed UAE LNG exports are still flowing despite Strait of Hormuz risk, providing a partial offset, though Iran's rejection of Oman's proposal to share Hormuz lane control signals the diplomatic path remains closed. Henry Hub was comparatively subdued, gaining 2.18% to $2.72/MMBtu but remaining down 14.5% on the month, reflecting loose domestic balances. Taiwan's suspension of roughly $800 million in spot LNG purchases from Papua New Guinea added a demand-side wrinkle, with implications for Pacific Basin price discovery.
drivers: TTF surged on sustained Hormuz supply-disruption risk; Iran's rejection of Oman's lane-sharing proposal removes a near-term diplomatic resolution
ADNOC confirmed UAE LNG flows continue, capping the upside and preventing a more severe European supply panic
Taiwan halted ~$800M in spot LNG purchases from Papua New Guinea, reshaping near-term Pacific Basin demand flows

power.summary: The power and carbon complex was relatively quiet against the backdrop of oil's surge. EU EUAs were essentially flat on the day at $78.00/EUA (+0.01%), though the weekly trend remains soft (-4.6%), likely reflecting near-term demand uncertainty. The higher TTF print (€60.5/MWh, +4.8%) will feed through into gas-fired generation costs and could support carbon prices if fuel-switching dynamics tighten. A headline from July 28 noted a drone attack on a UAE nuclear power plant, underscoring infrastructure vulnerability in the Gulf. The World Nuclear Association flagged a $6 trillion investment gap to meet 2050 capacity goals, reinforcing long-term energy security concerns. Ofgem launched a consultation on commitment fees for data center grid connections, a regulatory move targeting speculative capacity reservations that have strained UK grid planning.
drivers: EU EUAs barely moved (+0.01%) despite broader energy market turmoil; the week-on-week decline of 4.6% reflects lingering demand softness
Drone attack on a UAE nuclear power plant (reported July 28) highlights escalating infrastructure risk in the Gulf region
Ofgem's proposed data center grid commitment fees signal growing regulatory pressure on large power demand-side actors in the UK
